developments.dropped: The death toll is given as two by one outlet and three by another for the same period, and the accounts of the individual deaths differ in detail; both figures are stated above rather than one being chosen. The 272 mm figure is cited without a site or accumulation period by the source that reports it and is therefore not usable as a measurement.

salience.direction_note: Falling, and for the first time in this digest's run the judgement rests on something other than the two standing absences. The absences held for a fifth checkpoint. What is new is that the Dutch research interface to this field — which has been the one reliably active part of the Dutch lane — published six items in the week and none of them touched climate, water or food security. A country can be slow to commit and still be thinking; this was a week in which the thinking also went elsewhere. One positive instrument was found and it is dated: a parliamentary motion asking the government to hold a first Dutch briefing on climate, nature and security during 2026, which gives the lane a deadline ten weeks away.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The Hague strategic studies centre published six dated items in the week to 16 October — a study on Dutch exposure in semiconductor chokepoints, a piece on critical minerals between Canada and Europe, a satellites podcast, a media round-up, a guest-lecture note and a conference notice — and nothing from its climate, water and food security programme. Its October output to date is semiconductors, polysilicon, critical minerals and alliance contingency planning. Three months and two weeks after its own critique of the defence climate strategy asked for hard milestones and named climate, weather and ocean data as an unaddressed dependency, that argument has no follow-up from the institution that made it.

source.title: The Hague Centre for Strategic Studies, publications and news

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: A gewijzigde motie by Felix Klos and others, tabled on 3 March 2026 as 36800-XXIII-53 and replacing 36800-XXIII-22 of 12 February, asks the government to organise a first Dutch briefing on climate, nature and security during 2026, with the national counter-terrorism and security coordinator and outside experts. That is the most specific dated Dutch ask on this subject this digest has found, and the year it names has ten weeks left.

source.title: Gewijzigde motie van het lid Klos c.s. over een eerste Nederlandse briefing klimaat, natuur en veiligheid organiseren

claims.label: gap
claims.text: Whether that motion was adopted could not be established. The chamber's own pages list it under the votes of 3 March and give no result, and the published vote lists and stenographic record could not be opened. An unadopted motion is not an indicator and an adopted one with an unmet deadline is a strong one, so the difference matters and is not asserted here.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: The defence climate strategy's action plan has still not appeared — three months and fifteen days after the strategy of 3 July promised concrete measures, responsibilities and timelines. The EUR 5 million structural line from 2027 stands in the budget and remains the only costed climate-security item in it, against costed sustainable-fuel shares, a smart-grid trial and EUR 50 million as a first tranche for remediation at thirteen locations.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: No cabinet response to the deltacommissaris's 2027 programme was found, a fifth checkpoint passed in silence against a one-day turnaround in 2025, and nothing on water in the responsible committee inside the week. The parliamentary budget rounds on infrastructure and water fall later in the autumn, so part of this remains calendar; five checkpoints is well past the point where calendar explains it.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: Nothing was found from Dutch insurers, the ports, the grid operator or the water-technology sector connecting climate risk to security in the week. The one Dutch private-sector-adjacent contribution located is in measurement rather than in risk pricing: the national meteorological institute is a partner in the attribution network that published B7.

claims.label: framing
claims.text: The sentence the Union adopted on 12 October — climate change as an existential threat to peace and security — is now a Dutch position too, agreed in Council with Dutch participation. Hold it against the Dutch ledger this digest keeps: EUR 5 million a year with no spending plan, US$1 million to a regional fund, absence from the fourteen governments funding the UN's joint climate-security programme, and no national briefing on the subject yet held. The gap between what a government has agreed to say and what it has agreed to spend is the whole Dutch lane.

salience.method_note: The chamber was in session and the week contained no recess, so the Dutch silences are not calendar artefacts. The institute's own site was read directly; the Dutch institute whose climate-security platform this digest also tracks could not be read at its own address for a sixth consecutive week, though its output was found elsewhere — see the roster note and D3.

salience.direction_note: Mixed, and the mixture is now a settled division of labour rather than a tension. In the week the Union both adopted the field's strongest sentence — climate change as an existential threat to peace and security — and demonstrated, three days later and one institutional level up, that the sentence has no purchase where security is actually decided. Both things are in adopted texts, both are quotable, and they are about as far apart as two Union documents can be in one week.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The adopted COP31 conclusions of 12 October name climate change an existential threat to humanity, ecosystems and biodiversity "as well as to peace and security", and make early-warning availability a key component of climate resilience, especially for small island developing states and least developed countries. This is a Council mandate, not a communication or a speech.

source.title: Council conclusions on preparations for COP31, 14250/26

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The European Council's conclusions of 15 and 16 October run to twenty-one pages, devote a section to defence readiness and a paragraph to urgently strengthening resilience, preparedness and critical-infrastructure protection, and attach every named threat to a deliberate adversary act. Climate appears three times in the document: once on the carbon market, twice on whether all member states will be equally admitted to the Antalya conference.

source.title: European Council conclusions, EUCO 14/26

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: On resource commitment the position is now settled and negative. The adopted conclusions contain no new finance commitment; they cross-refer to the finance conclusions of 9 October, restate the New Collective Quantified Goal and the at-least-US$300-billion-a-year global goal, and record that developed countries provided and mobilised US$132.8 billion in 2023 and US$136.7 billion in 2024. The Union will arrive at Antalya as the largest provider of public climate finance with nothing new to offer, which is a coherent position and a hard one to carry into a room that has named finance as the test.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: No Union security institution appears in either climate text, and no climate referent appears in the security text. Nothing from the external action service or the High Representative was found inside the week; the foreign ministers' dialogue on climate change and ecosystem degradation as national security risks, held on 24 September, is now four weeks without institutional follow-through.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: Still no public institution estimate of what Europe's 2026 heat season cost. The only figure in circulation remains an insurer's proprietary model — about EUR 113 billion of annual output across thirty countries — and the statistical office, the environment agency and the national meteorological services have converted nothing. The integrated climate resilience framework is due on 28 October and is expected to carry an insurance architecture; if it does so without specifying an independent basis for loss estimation, the private number becomes the official one by default, and the deadline is now ten days away.

claims.label: framing
claims.text: The charitable account of the week is that environment ministers own the file and said what needed saying. The uncharitable one is that the Union has discovered how to hold a securitised climate position at zero cost: assert the threat in the instrument that spends nothing and commits no agency, and keep it out of the instrument that ranks priorities and allocates. On the evidence of this week the uncharitable account predicts the texts better. The test is 28 October.

salience.method_note: Both texts were read in full rather than from press summaries, and the three occurrences of "climate" in the European Council's conclusions are a direct count of the adopted document. The Council's press pages themselves would not open; the documents were read through the public document register instead.

salience.direction_note: No change, and the stable absence now has an external consequence attached to it for the first time. No federal climate-security observable was found inside the week — no rule, no hearing, no strategy, no statement from the defence, homeland security or intelligence establishments, in either direction. What did surface is the downstream effect of a decision taken nine months ago: the panel whose budget was left unresolved in Addis Ababa lost its American participation and funding in January, and a budget that cannot be set is the first dated consequence of that withdrawal to appear in this digest.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: On 7 January 2026 the United States announced withdrawal from sixty-six international organisations including the UN climate convention and the climate panel, ceasing participation and funding "to the extent permitted by law". The panel's response was that participation in its work is voluntary and open to all member countries with or without a formal announcement. Nine months later its 2027 budget is unset and it must reconvene before the end of the year to set one.

source.title: Withdrawal from UNFCCC and IPCC sidelines U.S. from key global decision-making

claims.label: gap
claims.text: Nothing from the American defence establishment in either direction for a ninth consecutive week. The standing pattern — installations hardened against extreme weather while the climate referent is removed from planning language — produced no new instance and no reversal.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The American climate-security institute published no climate research in the week. Its one new item, posted 15 October, announces an event for 27 October titled "Charging Forward: Electric Vehicles as Defense Technology", moderated by its director Erin Sikorsky with two of its non-resident fellows, arguing that advanced batteries are "a chokepoint technology on par with semiconductors", that China dominates the supply chain, that defence procurement alone cannot sustain a competitive American battery industry, and that without a domestic electric-vehicle market the United States risks "ceding a technology central to its future military capability". There is no climate content in the framing. Four consecutive weeks without a state-level briefer.

source.publisher: Center for Climate and Security, Council on Strategic Risks

claims.label: framing
claims.text: That reframing deserves credit before it gets scepticism: it is a serious argument, it is probably correct about batteries, and it is the register in which an American audience will currently fund work. It is also no longer climate security. A climate-security institute whose output this month is an industrial-policy case for electric vehicles and a 2030 geoengineering scenario has not stopped working; it has stopped doing the thing this digest tracks, and the displacement is the finding.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: No American polling on climate and security was published inside the week, and none was found from any institution. This is the fourth consecutive week with no public-opinion observable in this jurisdiction.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: Nothing found connecting American private-sector climate exposure to security in the week — no insurer, utility, reinsurer or ratings statement, and nothing from the reinsurance market on the El Nino now producing the flooding in B4, in a season its own models price.

salience.method_note: No federal shutdown or recess was in effect inside the week; the absence is not a calendar artefact. The withdrawal of January 2026 is recorded here because its consequence is dated to this week, not because it is new; a claim circulating in coverage that the United States had been the panel's largest funder is dropped at B1 for want of any source.

salience.direction_note: Mixed for the first time in nine weeks, and the change is in what can be observed rather than in what China is doing. On the security axis the answer is unchanged and now firmly established in the negative: no defence white paper, no doctrinal text, nothing. But China is a named party to the most consequential climate decision of the week, on the side that prevailed by preventing a decision, and this is the first time the position has been sourced to a wire service's own reporting from the room rather than to a specialist newsletter.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: China is reported among the states arguing for the later assessment timetable at the climate panel, with India, Kenya, Russia and Saudi Arabia, on the stated ground that scientists and governments in less-resourced countries need more time to research, review and approve the reports. The session ended with no decision, which is that group's preferred outcome obtained without a vote, for the sixth consecutive session.

source.title: Top global climate science body suspends meeting without deal on major review timeline

claims.label: gap
claims.text: Ninth consecutive week without any Chinese defence white paper, doctrinal text or military publication addressing climate. The instrument has now been tried for long enough to say the answer is not timing: Chinese climate positions are taken in science governance and in water diplomacy, and this digest should stop expecting a doctrinal text and keep working the two venues where positions are actually taken.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: The expert-level mechanism on trans-border rivers, which China's own foreign ministry text of the 25 August boundary talks committed both sides to convening in September with hydrological data sharing and renewal of the relevant memoranda on the agenda, has still not met. Third consecutive week of looking and nothing from either foreign ministry, either water ministry, or reporting in either country — two months past a dated bilateral undertaking. Reporting indicates the flood-season data window under the arrangement runs to 15 October, which fell inside this week; that date is from secondary reporting of an expired memorandum and is not asserted as current treaty practice.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: One Chinese contribution to this week's record is scientific and cooperative: the mountain centre's China office is a partner in the joint field mission that began this week on the Gyirong-Rasuwa corridor, which is the Chinese side of the border where 43 died and 519 are missing. A joint technical mission across that border is a real observable and it is the only form of Chinese climate-security cooperation this digest has been able to document.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: Nothing found linking Chinese private-sector or state-owned enterprise climate exposure to security. The nearest thing in the week's record is an American institute's argument that China dominates the battery supply chain, which is a claim about Chinese industrial strength made in Washington rather than a Chinese position.

salience.method_note: The security axis was checked at the defence ministry and in official military publications; the two substitute instruments — the trans-border rivers mechanism and the panel's plenary — were checked at both foreign ministries and in session reporting. Chinese-language primary sources were not read, which is a standing limit on this entry and should be read as one.

salience.direction_note: Mixed, with the same shape as the previous four weeks — active where finance, technology and water are transacted, absent where security is — and one thing newly settled. The 1996 Ganges treaty's expiry date, which this digest has reported as disputed between 12 and 31 December, is 12 December 2026. That now rests on the treaty's own text rather than on reporting, and it makes this the largest dated transboundary water decision in the field's calendar, eight weeks out.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The treaty on sharing of the Ganga/Ganges waters at Farakka was done at New Delhi on 12 December 1996 and signed by Sheikh Hasina and H. D. Deve Gowda. Article XII: "This Treaty shall enter into force upon signature and shall remain in force for a period of thirty years and it shall be renewable on the basis of mutual consent." Thirty years from signature expires on 12 December 2026, and renewal is not automatic. The sharing formula at Annexure I: at 70,000 cusecs or less at Farakka, an even split; between 70,000 and 75,000, Bangladesh takes 35,000 and India the balance; at 75,000 or more, India takes 40,000 and Bangladesh the balance — subject to each side receiving a guaranteed 35,000 cusecs in alternate three ten-day periods between 11 March and 10 May. Article II(iii): if flow at Farakka falls below 50,000 cusecs in any ten-day period the two governments "will enter into immediate consultations to make adjustments on an emergency basis, in accordance with the principles of equity, fair play and no harm to either party."

source.title: Treaty between the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and the Government of the Republic of India on sharing of the Ganga/Ganges waters at Farakka

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: India's external affairs ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said on 9 or 10 October that all discussions on river and water matters with Bangladesh take place within the ambit of the Joint Rivers Commission and that technical-level meetings have continued. Bangladesh's water resources minister Md Shahiduddin Chowdhury Anee has said Dhaka wants a new or revised agreement with an explicit guarantee of its share and hopes it will be completed before expiry. Dhaka has formed its own technical committee and is reported to have approached Delhi repeatedly without a response.

source.title: The Ganges Waters Treaty: Uncertain Prospects for Renewal
source.publisher: Amit Ranjan, Institute of South Asian Studies, National University of Singapore; republished by Eurasia Review

claims.label: contested
claims.text: What a renewal would have to fix is genuinely disputed and the dispute is on the record from named people on both sides. Manjur Chowdhury, chairman of Bangladesh's river conservation commission, calls the treaty "three decades old and flawed". Farooq Sobhan, the former Bangladeshi foreign secretary who negotiated it, says the absent arbitration clause is the problem and that India promised a barrage on the Padma as a trade-off: "But that barrage was not built." Sanjay Kumar Jha, a coalition-party president on the Indian side, calls for fresh negotiations. The live disagreements are dry-season allocation, treaty duration, measurement method, the dispute mechanism, and whether to move towards basin-wide governance.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: Ninth consecutive week without any Indian security or defence document addressing climate, and a fourth week with no response from Delhi to Nepal's 24 September proposal for a Himalayan climate resilience mechanism led by Nepal, India and China.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: An Indian institute did supply the week's best explanation for that silence, and it is in D3: a workshop report arguing that shared climate vulnerability in South Asia does not generate collective action, because climate governance remains national and sectorally siloed, sovereignty and information-sharing sensitivities shape what can be proposed, and material asymmetries mean states facing the same hazard set different priorities. Read against the unanswered Nepali proposal and the unmet China-India river mechanism, that is a finding rather than a lament.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: Nothing found from Indian insurers, industry bodies or state enterprises linking climate risk to security. The only figure in circulation remains an insurer's proprietary model putting India third globally at about US$50 billion of El Nino-related output loss concentrated in 2027, which is a commercial estimate and not an Indian position.

salience.method_note: The treaty text was obtained and read, as this digest's standing instruction required, rather than taking the expiry date from reporting. Joint Rivers Commission meeting records and West Bengal's correspondence with Delhi were not located and are not characterised; the Indian ministry statement is reported from agency coverage of a briefing, not from a ministry transcript.

salience.direction_note: Falling, and this is the first week in this digest's run where that word is the right one for the multilateral lane rather than "mixed". The scientific institution could not set a timetable or a budget and did not set a date to try again. The Security Council held a sixth straw poll on the succession with the first colour-coded ballots in the process's history and no convergence, eleven weeks from the end of the incumbent's term, and nobody has yet asked any candidate a public question about climate. Against that, one institution moved in the other direction and it is the smallest and newest: a fund board called its first-ever extraordinary meeting.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The climate panel's sixty-fifth plenary was suspended on 16 October with the assessment timetable and the budget both open and no resumption date. The practical consequence is in B1: the second global stocktake may have to run on special reports and the published literature rather than on a full assessment cycle, and the 2027 budget is unset.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The sixth straw poll on the succession was held on Friday 16 October with China and the United States as tellers, appointed on 14 October, and used colour-coded ballots for the first time — red for the five permanent members, white for the ten elected — so that a permanent member's discouragement is legible. Reporting gives Rebeca Grynspan first with nine encourage and five discourage but opposed by two permanent members, Rafael Grossi and Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett at eight encourage and six discourage each and also opposed by two permanent members, and Ivonne A-Baki discouraged by all five. Nine encourage and no permanent-member veto is the threshold. Nobody withdrew and nobody new entered.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: Nothing found on the climate position of any of the seven candidates, from the Council, from the General Assembly's dialogues, or from their own material. Sixth consecutive poll with the question unasked in public. What the week did produce is a regional claim: a letter from the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States (CELAC) on 13 October arguing that "the time has come for a national of Latin America and the Caribbean" and asking the Council and the Assembly to give the region's position due consideration — a letter about geography rather than about any policy.

source.title: Sixth Security Council Straw Poll on UN Secretary-General Candidates

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The one institution moving towards this field is the loss and damage fund, and the numbers show why that is a qualified comfort: a draft decision to set aside US$20 million for Nepal, before a board considering 180 proposals worth about US$2.8 billion with about US$350 million to allocate, taking about forty-five days to organise the extraordinary meeting at which it will be taken. See D1.

source.title: UN's loss and damage fund set to give Nepal $20m for flood recovery

claims.label: gap
claims.text: The Security Council's October programme of work carries no climate, water, food-security or environment item in any framing, and the month is now two-thirds gone. The joint seminar with the African Union on 21 and 22 October is the only remaining route, and a food-security or climate framing there would be the African Union's to bring rather than a Council member's. Nothing from any other multilateral security body: no alliance statement, no peace-operations climate item, nothing from the disarmament machinery.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: No multilateral institution produced any assessment of private climate exposure this week. The only pricing of climate damage in multilateral circulation remains an insurer's proprietary model, and the one multilateral figure that did surface this week is an aggregate of practitioner self-reports: almost US$120 million of anticipatory money released worldwide in 2025 — see the pushback, where it corrects this publication.

claims.label: framing
claims.text: The pattern across the three items is one institution. The panel protects consensus by not deciding; the Council protects the appearance of consensus by colour-coding a ballot so that dissent is visible without being attributable; the fund protects its mandate by piloting an out-of-cycle window rather than changing its rules. In each case a procedural device is substituting for a decision nobody can take, and in each case the device is a reasonable response to a real constraint. The question for this field is what happens to an evidentiary chain — assessed science to best-available-science standard to fund decision — when every link is held together by a procedural device.

salience.method_note: The Council's own announcements were not opened; the straw-poll procedure and the tellers come from the Council monitor's forward note of 15 October and the results from press reporting of a leaked outcome, which is how every poll in this process has become public. The panel's own pages would not open. The fund's draft decision is reported from a specialist wire's reading of the document, not from the document.

moves.title: The loss and damage fund's board calls the first extraordinary meeting in its existence, to set aside US$20 million for Nepal
moves.actor: Board members of the Fund responding to Loss and Damage, from developed and developing country constituencies, drafting jointly; the co-chairs convening
moves.place: Reported from the draft decision; the meeting is set for 22 October
moves.body: A draft decision reported on 16 October would have the board "provisionally set aside" US$20 million for Nepal to deal with the effects of the 26 August flood, and invite the government of Nepal to submit a proposal for how to use it, with approval to follow at a regular board meeting. One Kathmandu report gives the figure as US$21.6 million including US$1.6 million of oversight fees; the difference appears to be the fee and was not confirmed. The decision is to be taken at the fund's first-ever extraordinary board meeting, on 22 October. The motion was drafted by board members from both constituencies and is expected to pass easily. Its procedural content is the larger part: Nepal's proposal would pilot a mechanism for submitting funding requests outside the fund's regular call-for-proposals timetable, so that a government could seek money soon after a disaster rather than waiting for the next window. The arithmetic around it is unforgiving. The fund has run exactly one call for proposals, launched at Belém in November 2025 with a six-month application period; it is considering 180 proposals costing about US$2.8 billion in total and has about US$350 million to allocate; it has not yet awarded any money. Nepali officials have called the US$20 million symbolic against an estimated US$4.8 billion of recovery and reconstruction cost. The sequence took forty-five days: ministers wrote on 31 August, developing-country board members asked for an extraordinary meeting, developed-country members initially proposed an informal consultation instead, and the meeting and motion were organised over about six weeks.
moves.stated_rationale: Urgency, in Nepal's own words to the board — "time is of the essence" — and, in the draft decision's construction, the testing of a route by which a government can request money outside the fund's regular cycle. The campaign group Fill the Fund calls the draft "a real step forward" and "the first time this Fund has moved to respond to a specific disaster", while saying US$20 million "is a meaningful signal" but "a drop against an ocean of need", and that "Speed must be built in, not improvised."
moves.inference:
Three things are happening at once and only one of them is about Nepal.

The first is that the fund has found a way to act without deciding the question it exists to answer. Setting money aside provisionally, and inviting a proposal to be approved later, converts an emergency claim into a normal application with a reserved line — which is administratively sound and means the board does not have to say, this month, what standard of evidence a claim from an event with no event-level attribution has to meet. That question has been open in this digest since 13 September and it stays open. The draft does not mention attribution, adaptation limits or causation, and six days before the meeting the evidentiary ground under the claim moved anyway, in B2, in a direction nobody at the board asked for.

The second is that this is a precedent being set in its smallest possible form. The out-of-cycle window is the real content, it is what every future claimant will cite, and it is being piloted on an event with 1,451 dead and 5,745 missing, at a figure its recipient calls symbolic, against a cost its own officials put four hundred times higher. A precedent set at that ratio establishes that the route exists and simultaneously establishes what travels down it.

The third is the comparison the field should hold on to. Forty-five days to organise one meeting; 180 proposals for US$2.8 billion against US$350 million available; nothing disbursed since the fund was agreed in 2022. Set that beside the week's other number, from the pushback: almost US$120 million released worldwide in a year of anticipatory action. The two instruments the field offers for climate loss — money before the event and money after it — are, between them, operating at a scale of low hundreds of millions of dollars a year globally, which is the order of magnitude of a mid-sized European flood-defence contract. The argument about whether either works is downstream of that.

moves.title: The panel's chair suspends a plenary rather than decide without the delegations that had gone home
moves.actor: Jim Skea, Chair of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change
moves.body: On the evening of Friday 16 October, with the session already past its scheduled close and with delegations from least developed countries and small island developing states having left, the chair suspended the sixty-fifth plenary instead of putting the assessment timetable or the budget to the room. The panel's statement frames the decision as upholding inclusivity in a body whose major decisions are taken by consensus, and says both items remain open with deliberations to resume at the earliest opportunity. No resumption date was given. The review of the panel's own principles and procedures was deferred for a further session, as were the summaries of three earlier meetings. This is the second time in two sessions that the chair has chosen a procedural route over a contested decision: at Bangkok in March he proposed an options paper, then proposed postponing all timeline deliberations to this session, and was opposed on the second by seventeen states.
moves.stated_rationale: Inclusivity. The panel's own wording is that the chair's decision is intended to uphold the principle of inclusivity in its plenaries, where governments make major decisions through consensus, and that the meeting had run over its planned duration with many delegations from the least developed countries and small island developing states already departed.
moves.inference:
Take the stated rationale seriously, because it is correct on its own terms and because the alternative was worse. A decision on the timetable for the assessment that the most exposed states depend on, taken in a room those states had left because the session overran, would have been both procedurally defective and politically indefensible, and it would have been quoted against the panel for a decade. The chair was handed a choice between a bad decision and no decision and took no decision.

That does not make the consequence neutral, and the asymmetry is the point. In this dispute one side wants a date and the other wants later; no decision is later. Six consecutive sessions have now ended without a decision, and at each one the procedural outcome has matched the substantive preference of the group that prefers delay, without that group having to carry the cost of blocking anything. A consensus rule plus an overrunning agenda is a veto that nobody has to cast, and the states most disadvantaged by it are the ones whose departure made the suspension necessary. The Marshall Islands envoy's phrase — "a shameful play for time when there is no time to waste" — is about the room, not about the chair, and is the sharpest thing a small-state representative has said in this digest's run since the Pacific's objection in September.

One further reading, offered as speculation and labelled as such. The budget is the pressure point, not the timetable: the panel must reconvene before the end of the year to set a 2027 budget, and a body whose expenditures have exceeded contributions and whose largest-economy participant withdrew in January has less room to absorb another deadlock than it had in March. If the two items are bundled at the resumed session, the side that can live without a 2028 report has a hostage, and the side that wants the report has a deadline. That is a worse configuration for the earlier timetable than this week's outcome looks.

moves.title: An Indian and a Dutch institute publish the case against assuming that shared climate vulnerability produces cooperation
moves.actor: Institute of Peace and Conflict Studies, New Delhi, with the Clingendael Institute; foreword by IPCS director Ruhee Neog
moves.place: New Delhi and The Hague; from a workshop at Kochi, India, in May 2026
moves.body: Published on 12 October as IPCS Special Report 227, *Shared Vulnerability, Divided Action: South Asia's Climate Paradox*, from a track 1.5 workshop at Kochi in May 2026 that included a simulation exercise on regional climate governance. Its argument is directed at the field's most comfortable assumption. Climate risk crosses borders, the report says, and cooperation continues to be driven by national interest; climate governance remains national and divided across sectoral silos, which limits integrated responses to climate risks and their social, economic and security effects; uneven vulnerabilities, capacities and resources lead states to hold different expectations of what regional cooperation is for; and sensitivities about sovereignty, information sharing and representation shape what can be proposed. Participants questioned whether existing regional institutions can handle complex transboundary challenges at all. The conclusion the report draws is the uncomfortable one: proposals get designed around political feasibility rather than around what the risks require, and designing for feasibility is easier to start and less useful once started. It offers nine observations against which a new institutional design can be tested, and the report's own framing is that weakening multilateralism may push the region towards stronger self-organisation, making climate change both a challenge to and an opportunity for regionalism.
moves.stated_rationale: That cooperation efforts must start from an honest account of the region's political and institutional realities, and that policymakers should not assume shared vulnerability will automatically produce collective action, but design mechanisms that work within existing constraints while responding to interconnected risks.
moves.inference:
Two reasons this is a move and not a publication.

The first is what it does to three open questions in this digest. Nepal proposed a Himalayan climate resilience mechanism from the General Assembly rostrum on 24 September and has had no answer from Delhi or Beijing in four weeks. The China-India expert mechanism on trans-border rivers is two months past a dated commitment to meet. The Ganges treaty expires on 12 December with the two governments describing the state of play in incompatible terms. This digest has been recording those as three separate silences. The report's claim is that they are one structural feature, that the feature is not reducible to any current government's disposition, and that an unanswered regional proposal is the normal output of the system rather than a failure within it. If that is right, the thing to watch is not whether Delhi replies but what institutional form a proposal would have to take to be repliable.

The second is institutional, and it is about who was able to say it. This is a Dutch institute's output, co-produced with an Indian one, published through a platform rather than through its own site — which this digest has been unable to open for six consecutive weeks and had therefore been scoring as unassessable. The institute is not quiet. It is working on the file this digest has found hardest to make legible, from the Indian end, with Indian co-authors, and the only reason that was invisible is that the route was wrong. Note also the asymmetry in the authorship: the report names its Indian contributors and does not name individual authors from the Dutch side, and the Dutch contribution is described as a project partnership. What the Dutch institute supplied is reach rather than argument, which is the same pattern the Dutch lane in C keeps producing at every scale.

moves.title: The alliance's climate centre convenes the defence-investment summit it has been building towards, and publishes nothing about it
moves.actor: NATO Climate Change and Security Centre of Excellence, Montreal, with the Conference of Defence Associations Institute
moves.body: The fifth Montreal Climate Security Summit was announced by both hosts for 15 and 16 October, by invitation only, titled *Resilient Defence: Climate-Smart Investments on the Road to 5%* — the road being the alliance's Hague commitment of 5 per cent of national output by 2035, of which 1.5 points are defence- and security-related including resilience. Nine themes were published: climate-resilience metrics and standards for defence procurement, financing and costing climate-smart defence, climate intelligence in defence planning, defence industrial strategies, critical minerals and clean energy supply chains, climate-resilient infrastructure and bases, personnel health and readiness in extreme environments, operational energy, and public-private partnership. The published speaker list is the most informative part and crosses every boundary this digest tracks: the chief of staff for infrastructure and environment of the Canadian Armed Forces; the British Army's head of productivity and sustainability; a NATO armaments director and a NATO defence policy and planning officer; the Norwegian ambassador to Canada; the secretary general of the International Military Council on Climate and Security; the head of EU and global affairs at the Dutch institute whose own site this digest cannot open; the American climate-security institute's director emeritus; the director of its parent's converging risks laboratory; the European external action service's climate special envoy; and analysts from a British defence laboratory, a German climate service centre, a European economics institute and the aerospace industry. A Nordic resilience and infrastructure workshop was listed for 14 October alongside it. As of 19 October neither host has published any account, communique or recap of the event.
moves.stated_rationale: To explore, through plenary panels, workshops, roundtables and wargames, how allied defence establishments should invest the climate-relevant portion of a rising defence budget — explicitly framed around the 5 per cent commitment rather than around climate risk as such.
moves.inference:
On the substance, this is the argument the military council made in an open letter on 23 October 2025 — that clean energy investment should count inside the alliance's non-core defence spending — reappearing as a two-day programme with industry, armaments directors and investors in the room, convened by an alliance body rather than by an advocacy council. That is the shape a position takes when it wins: it loses its author and becomes a procurement conversation. It is also the answer to the risk this digest flagged when the conference presidency priced the climate finance ask against the 5 per cent defence commitment. The counter-move to "spend on climate like you spend on defence" is "we already do, inside the 1.5 points", and this summit is where the accounting for that claim is being built. Climate-resilience metrics for defence procurement is precisely the instrument that would let a treasury book resilience spending against both ledgers.

On the silence, the comparison is the evidence and it is narrow. This digest's standing rule for a dated fixture is to score only a disconfirmation, and there is none: both hosts' own pages carried the event. But the centre published a recap of the 2024 edition on 30 October 2024 and of the 2025 edition on 15 October 2025 — within or immediately after each event — and has published nothing on this one three days after it closed. Its news stream for 2026 consists of two items, a spring course in May and a welcome to its fellows on 6 October. An invitation-only summit whose theme is how to spend a defence budget may simply be less publishable than one about dialogue, and a centre with a nine-track programme and no publications has a staffing constraint rather than a position. Both readings are available and this digest cannot separate them this week. What it can say is that the alliance's climate work is now conducted where it is least legible: not in the annual public assessment that stopped after 2024, nor in the baseline requirements from which the climate referent was removed in September, but in an invitation-only room in Montreal.

moves.title: The Security Council colour-codes a straw poll for the first time, making a veto visible without making it attributable
moves.actor: The Security Council under the presidency of Greece; China and the United States appointed as tellers on 14 October
moves.body: The sixth straw poll on the succession to the Secretary-General was held on Friday 16 October and, unlike the five before it, used colour-coded ballots: red for the five permanent members and white for the ten elected, each listing the candidates with "encouraged", "discouraged" and "no opinion expressed". A red "discouraged" is a strong signal of a potential veto, though it can be reversed. The presidency was expected to confirm only that the poll took place; the results leaked, as they have after every round. Reporting gives Rebeca Grynspan first with nine encourage and five discourage but two permanent members against; Rafael Grossi and Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett on eight encourage and six discourage, each with two permanent members against; and Ivonne A-Baki discouraged by all five. All seven candidates remain and none is new. The incumbent's term ends on 31 December. Minh-Thu Pham of the Starling Institute called the gap between the top three "very, very slim" and the outcome "a split decision with no P5 convergence"; the American ambassador, Mike Waltz, said the priority was "the best candidate" rather than regional rotation or gender, and is reported to think the Council can finish before the end of 2026. On 13 October the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States wrote arguing that "the time has come for a national of Latin America and the Caribbean".
moves.stated_rationale: Not stated. The Council does not explain its straw-poll procedure, and the presidency's practice is to confirm only that a poll occurred. The purpose colour-coding serves is structural: it lets the fourteen other members, and through the leak everyone else, see whether a candidate's discouragement sits with a permanent member, without any permanent member having to say so.
moves.inference:
This belongs in a climate security digest for one reason and it is not the succession. For six consecutive polls, across eleven weeks, this digest has looked for any public question put to any of the seven candidates about climate, or about whether the Council has competence over it, and found none — from the Council, from the Assembly's dialogues, or from the candidates' own material. The institution that vetoed a climate-security resolution in December 2021 is choosing the official who would have to carry the file for the next five years, and the question has not been asked once in public.

The colour-coding is the week's novelty and it cuts both ways. It makes obstruction legible, which is a real transparency gain, and it makes obstruction cheap, because a red ballot is anonymous within the five. Compare the device to the one in D2: a consensus rule that lets a group get delay without casting a veto, and a colour-coded ballot that lets a permanent member signal a veto without owning it. In the same week, two multilateral institutions reached for procedural devices that preserve a decision's appearance while removing anyone's name from it. For a field whose entire theory of change is that the right argument put to the right institution produces a decision, that is the more durable finding.

roster_silences:
Worked this week, and the roster produced one correction to method that matters more than any of the silences.

**The correction.** The Dutch institute whose climate-security platform this digest tracks has been recorded for five weeks as unassessable, because its own address would not open. That stands as a retrieval problem and for a sixth week. It is no longer a statement about the institute's activity: through the platform it hosts, its co-authored report on South Asian climate cooperation appeared on 12 October (D3), and its head of EU and global affairs is on the published speaker list for the alliance centre's Montreal summit (D4). The institute is active on both of the files this digest has found hardest to work. The standing instruction — when a route fails three times, stop retrying and go find the sister site — was followed and worked, and the thing it revealed is that scoring the route as a hole in the method understated how much was being missed.

**Findings, under the rule that silence from a body with a published schedule is evidence.** The International Military Council has now been silent for twelve months and this week its silence acquired a venue: its secretary general appears on the speaker list of the alliance centre's Montreal summit, whose subject is the argument her council's open letter of 23 October 2025 made. Its publications index still ends at a February 2024 event summary and does not even list the 2023-24 edition of its own annual flagship, which exists; its media index ends in June 2023. A body with a named chair, a named secretary general and a standing report series is now participating in other people's programmes. Separately, the alliance's annual climate and security assessment remains unpublished since 2024 with no statement ever made about it, and the alliance centre has published nothing about the summit it convened this week against same-period recaps in 2024 and 2025 (D4).

**Lead time, not findings.** The Stockholm institute's climate, peace and security list still ends at the August Abyei study, with nothing for September or October. The Himalayan mountain centre is the week's exception and published twice (B2, B3). The attribution network published on a Pacific hurricane (B7) and nothing on the Horn of Africa season now under way or on Europe's heat season; no declined request was found, so that is case selection rather than refusal. The Hague strategic studies centre published six items and none on climate, water or food security (C, Netherlands). The American climate-security institute published no climate research and one event notice about electric vehicles as defence technology.

**Non-Western actors, worked as instructed.** China: nothing doctrinal, a ninth week; the trans-border rivers mechanism still unmet, a third week; one real cooperative observable in the joint Himalayan field mission. India: nothing doctrinal, a ninth week; an institute report that explains the pattern (D3); the Ganges treaty now dated. The African Union: nothing found inside the week, with the joint Security Council seminar of 21 and 22 October the next dated observable. The Gulf states: Saudi Arabia is reported among the states pressing for the later assessment timetable and nothing else was found. The small island states' alliance: not found speaking as an alliance this week, with the Marshall Islands' envoy and a regional caucus letter carrying small-state positions instead — which is the fourth consecutive week in which the constituency's positions are carried by individual states rather than by the bloc.

**Two additions to the standing roster, both from the week's own material.** The anticipatory-action community of practice that publishes the annual global count corrected in the pushback, because it holds the only public series on the field's central operational doctrine and this digest spent three weeks not finding it. And the alliance centre's co-host in Montreal, a Canadian defence association institute, because the speaker list it publishes is currently the most complete public map of who works on defence and climate across the alliance, and because one title on that list — the European external action service's climate envoy — is given there in a form no European source confirms.

watch.title: The loss and damage fund's first extraordinary board meeting
watch.note: Whether the board sets aside the US$20 million, and — the thing that will outlast it — whether the out-of-cycle submission route is adopted as a pilot with stated conditions or left as an ad hoc accommodation. Three subsidiary answers fall on the same day. Whether any board paper reasons from either of the week's two evidentiary findings: the hazard-environment attribution of September or the forty-eight-day precursor signal published on 13 October. Whether the decision text says anything at all about what standard a claim from an unattributed event must meet, which has been open here since 13 September. And whether the figure is US$20 million or US$21.6 million, which is a small question that settles whether oversight fees come out of the allocation or sit on top of it.

watch.title: The Security Council's joint seminar with the African Union
watch.note: The only remaining route by which a climate, water or food-security framing enters the Council's October programme, which otherwise carries none in any framing and closes on 31 October with four mandate renewals. What makes it worth watching rather than hoping for is whose framing it would be: the African Union's to bring, not a Council member's, in a month when the Horn of Africa is flooding and a famine risk is classified. If the seminar produces no climate content, the month closes with a Council that discussed children and armed conflict, maritime security and emerging technologies and not this, under a presidency that announced the succession as its substantive business.

watch.title: Whether the climate panel names a date, and whether Montreal produces a document
watch.note: Two silences with the same deadline, which is the opening of the Antalya conference. First: the panel must reconvene before the end of the year to set a 2027 budget, and the suspended session set no resumption date. Watch for a date, for whether the budget and the assessment timetable are bundled when it comes, and for any statement from the states on either side. Second: whether the alliance centre or its Canadian co-host publishes anything from the summit of 15 and 16 October — a communique, a recap, a reading of the nine tracks, anything. Both previous editions produced a recap within days. If this one produces nothing by the time the conference opens, then the proposition that the alliance's climate work has moved from public instruments into invitation-only rooms stops being an inference.
