active_trends.text: Removal of climate from security vehicles rather than only from language. The strongest instance yet, and it is European rather than American. The European Council's conclusions of 15 and 16 October run to twenty-one pages, devote a section to defence readiness and a paragraph to urgently strengthening resilience, preparedness and critical-infrastructure protection, and contain three occurrences of the word climate: one on the carbon market and two on whether all member states will be admitted to a conference. In the alliance's revised resilience baseline requirements of September the hazard survived and the word went; here neither appears. The American side produced nothing in either direction for a ninth week. The trend is no longer about one government's drafting discipline.

US adaptation surviving only where reframed as disaster operations. No federal observable for a ninth week, and at the institute level the reframing is now clearly not what is being pressed. A fourth week with no state-level briefer, and the only new output from the American climate-security institute is an event on electric vehicles as defence technology, arguing that batteries are a chokepoint technology on a par with semiconductors. The disaster-operations reframing has not failed; it has been displaced by supply-chain competition, which is a different argument with no adaptation content at all. This trend should probably be closed next week and replaced with one about where displaced climate-security capacity goes.

Security Council shift from climate security to natural resource governance, and now past it. Unchanged and two-thirds through the month that tests it: the October programme carries no climate, water, food-security or environment item in any framing, and the only remaining route is the joint seminar with the African Union on 21 and 22 October, where the framing would be the African Union's to bring. What the Council did do this week was colour-code a straw poll so that a permanent member's opposition is visible without being attributable, which is the institution's energy going into its own succession.

Retreat from binding multilateral environmental instruments, and it has now reached the thing that binds the instruments to reality. The panel's sixty-fifth plenary was suspended with the assessment timetable and the 2027 budget both open and no date set to resume. Nobody has proposed leaving anything. The effect of a two-year gap in assessed science, and now of a procedural deadlock with no scheduled next attempt, is to loosen every instrument that cites assessed science without any state having to withdraw from one. Six consecutive sessions, and the mechanism is a consensus rule plus an overrunning agenda.

Dutch institutional creation with fiscal non-commitment, and this week the pattern extended from money to attention. The EUR 5 million structural defence line stands and its action plan is three months and fifteen days overdue; no cabinet response on water at a fifth checkpoint. New this week: the Dutch research interface to this field published six items and none on climate, water or food security, while a parliamentary motion asking for a first national briefing on climate, nature and security during 2026 has ten weeks of its own deadline left and an outcome this digest could not establish. The pattern is not absence of money; it is commitments at an order of magnitude that cannot change an outcome, attached to positions that can be cited — and the Union sentence the Netherlands agreed to on 12 October is now the largest of those positions.

The assets a changing hazard environment destroys are increasingly publicly indispensable, and the question of who pays is still unsettled. Advanced on the public side this week: the asset at the centre of the second Himalayan flood is the 341 MW Budhi Gandaki hydropower project, state-owned and under construction, after 759 MW of damaged generation in August. Four consecutive Himalayan events in this digest's run in which generation capacity was the headline loss. On the instrument side, the only money moving is US$20 million provisionally set aside against a recovery cost its recipient's officials put at US$4.8 billion, which is a ratio rather than a mechanism.

The climate referent and the security register being decoupled, by venue rather than by actor, and this week one institution did both in four days. On 12 October the Union adopted a negotiating mandate calling climate change an existential threat "to humanity, ecosystems and biodiversity, as well as to peace and security". On 15 and 16 October its heads of government adopted twenty-one pages on defence, resilience and the Arctic in which climate appears three times, none of them substantively. The referent is not being removed and it is not even being routed between actors any more: it is being sorted by what a document commits. Where climate diplomacy is conducted the field's vocabulary is free; where security is decided it is absent.

The contest is moving from the hazard to the apparatus that measures and prices it, and this week the apparatus produced the week's two biggest findings and its biggest disagreement. A plenary could not agree when the measurement arrives or who pays for it. A mountain research centre, reading European radar, found a forty-eight-day precursor signal on the slope that killed 1,451 people, which contradicts the premise of the adaptation-limits conclusion drawn from the same event four weeks earlier. An attribution network measured warming and El Nino against one metric for one storm and reported the ratio. And a published argument in the field's own literature proposes shifting the default so that climate influence is presumed unless disproved. Every one of those is a claim about instruments, and three of the four will be cited in front of institutions that distribute money.

Forecast quality and institutional calendars have come apart, and this week the forecast started being right. The Shabelle at Jowhar crossed its high flood-risk level on 13 October, fourteen centimetres below bankfull, exactly where and roughly when the probabilities said it would. Against that: the collective flood anticipatory-action framework and its trigger protocols still unconfirmed as finalised, no district plans found, and a practitioner in the country saying preparedness and data are better than 2023 while funding and capacity have seriously decreased. One figure now exists that this digest said did not — almost US$120 million of anticipatory money released worldwide in 2025 — and it makes the mismatch worse rather than better: the calendars are not the only thing that has not moved to match the forecasts. Neither has the money.

The evidentiary question for climate loss is shifting from attribution to foreseeability, and the two answers are coming from different institutions about the same event. An attribution network concluded in September that the Himalayan cascade exceeded the predictive limits of existing risk reduction, that no early warning system could have provided sufficient lead time, and that this constituted a soft limit to adaptation. A mountain research centre published on 13 October that the slope had registered up to 40 cm of satellite-measurable movement over the forty-eight days before it failed, and that warnings reached the valley twenty-five to thirty minutes after the debris. Both can be true; detecting deformation is not predicting timing. But "nobody could have known" and "the signal was in the data for seven weeks" are different sentences in front of a fund, an insurer or a court, and a claim on the first disaster-specific loss and damage decision in history is live between them. What to watch is whether any obligor anywhere starts asking what was measurable rather than what was attributable, because the moment one does, every monitoring gap becomes a liability question and every monitoring investment becomes a defence.

open_threads.text: The Dutch institute's current funding phase. Unmoved as a question and the route has failed for a sixth week: the institute's own domain refused retrieval again. But the thread's framing needs separating from the institute's activity, which this week was visible elsewhere — a co-authored report on South Asian climate cooperation on 12 October and its head of EU and global affairs on a NATO centre's summit speaker list. The last publicly datable announcement of a funding phase for the platform remains December 2019. Six refusals is a statement about one route, and the sister-site route answers a different question; what this week establishes is that the institute is working on the two hardest files in this digest while its resourcing stays unreadable.

Whether the alliance published a fourth Climate Change and Security Impact Assessment. Still no, still no statement, and the displacing activity has now happened. The alliance's own climate change and security centre of excellence convened its Montreal summit on 15 and 16 October, by invitation, on how to spend the climate-relevant share of a rising defence budget, with a published speaker list spanning allied armed forces, NATO divisions, European and American institutes and the defence industry — and has published nothing about it as of 19 October, against recaps of the 2024 and 2025 editions within days of each. The alliance's climate work plainly continues. What stopped is the one public, citable, annual judgement, and what replaced it is a room.

Whether the International Military Council's World Climate and Security Report has formally lapsed. Seventh consecutive week of silence, and this week the silence has a location: its secretary general appears on the published speaker list of the alliance centre's Montreal summit, whose subject is the argument her own council's open letter of 23 October 2025 made. Its publications index still ends at a February 2024 event summary and does not list the 2023-24 edition of its own flagship, which exists elsewhere; its media index ends in June 2023. Twelve months without a report of any kind, and the position now travels without the body.
Funding trajectory of the joint United Nations climate security unit.
open_threads.resolution: Answered in magnitude, by a printed portfolio report rather than by the dashboard that has refused to render for three weeks. Cumulative deposits to the joint programme between 2016 and 2024 were $18.27 million, which places it thirteenth of fifteen funds in the trust fund office's climate and environment portfolio, against $808.89 million for the largest and about $2 million a year for this one. Fourteen governments contribute, eleven of them European; the Netherlands is not among them. The programme is not being wound down — a third phase runs 2026 to 2028 with ten advisers deployed — and it is funded at the level of a mid-sized national research grant. One consequence for this digest's own published record: Britain's £1 million of 25 September, reported here as three tenths of one per cent of a £331 million package and treated as a rounding error, is on the order of 5 per cent of everything this programme has ever received. The denominator was wrong. What remains unanswered is the year-by-year trajectory and whether the third phase has a stated requirement, which is carried forward as a separate question.

open_threads.text: Whether the 2028-2034 budget carries a security-tagged climate line. Not advanced internally and the external signals hardened. The Union's adopted negotiating mandate of 12 October contains no new finance commitment of any kind; the heads of government discussed the long-term budget on 15 and 16 October aiming for agreement by the end of 2026 so that legislation can pass in 2027, and did not mention climate in that context. The special European Council on the budget falls on 26 and 27 November. The nearer instrument, the integrated climate resilience framework of 28 October, is still expected to arrive with an insurance architecture rather than a budget line.

Chinese defence doctrine on climate — gap, ninth week, and this is the week to retire the instrument rather than keep reporting its emptiness. No white paper, no doctrinal text, nothing. The two substitutes are the venues where Chinese climate positions are actually taken: the trans-border rivers expert mechanism, now two months past a dated commitment to convene and unmet for a third consecutive week of checking, and the climate panel's assessment timetable, where China is reported among the states pressing for delivery after the 2028 stocktake and where this week's suspension delivered that outcome without a vote. One cooperative observable this week, and it is real: the mountain centre's China office is a partner in the joint field mission on the Gyirong-Rasuwa corridor.

Any Indian security document on climate — gap, ninth week, and the file is now legible without one. Three instruments carry it. India is reported among the states pressing for the later assessment timetable, which prevailed by suspension on 16 October. The Ganges treaty's expiry is now fixed at 12 December 2026 from the treaty text itself, with the two governments describing the state of negotiations in incompatible terms. And an Indian institute published, with a Dutch partner, the best available explanation of why the Indian security lane stays empty: climate governance in the region is national and sectorally siloed, and proposals get designed around political feasibility rather than around what the risks require.
Swiss Re sigma citation for the $424bn 2025 protection gap.
open_threads.resolution: The citation is **sigma 1/2026**, *Natural catastrophes in 2025: the persistent rise of wildfire and storm risk*, Swiss Re Institute. The protection gap of $424 billion for 2025, up from $395 billion in 2024, with the natural catastrophe resilience index broadly stable at 27.3 per cent, comes from the Institute's Natural Catastrophe Insurance Resilience Index and is expressed in premium-equivalent terms. Caveat on strength: the reinsurer's own page would not open and the mirrored PDF's text could not be extracted, so the figures are corroborated across Swiss Re's own social post and several independent trade reports rather than read off the document.

open_threads.text: Whether any event attribution study of the 26 August Langtang-Lirung cascade appears.
open_threads.resolution: Resolved on 17 September 2026, and the answer is not one of the two the thread was framed to expect. World Weather Attribution published *Rapid Warming in the Himalaya Exacerbates Geohazard Cascades Beyond Adaptation Limits*, with contributors in ten countries across glaciology, mountain hydrology, climate science, seismology, humanitarian practice and social science. It attributes the hazard environment and not the event: about 1.5°C added to July-August temperatures by human-caused climate change, about 2°C annually — larger than global mean warming — individual winter months as much as 3°C, and the 0°C isotherm rising roughly 100 metres a decade into the bedrock that failed. It states explicitly that it has not assessed whether this specific rock-ice avalanche would have occurred without human-induced climate change, while asserting that warming at a rate beyond the global mean increases the likelihood and severity of such hazards. It then concludes that the event exceeded the design and predictive limits of existing risk reduction, that no existing early warning system could have provided sufficient lead time, that this constitutes a soft limit to adaptation given constrained habitable land and population increase, and that addressing loss and damage through recovery and reconstruction has become an unavoidable part of climate response. So: no event attribution, a hazard-environment attribution, and the policy conclusion reached through adaptation limits instead of causation. The successor question is the `adaptation-limits-adjudication` thread. Reporting figures that travelled with it: the debris flood ran 200 km in under seven hours at average speeds around 188 km/h and deposited 30.5 million cubic metres of material.

open_threads.text: What the HiRISK consortium is: membership, funding, institutional home.
open_threads.resolution: Resolved from hirisk.org, which was opened and read. HiRISK describes itself as 'a loose consortium of experts from High Mountain Asia and beyond', producing open risk datasets, dashboards, an expert database, risk assessments and peer-reviewed papers. Its listed member organisations include the Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee, the University of Central Asia in Tajikistan, a research group in Pakistan, a mountain-hazards institute in China, a hydrological institute in Bhutan, and two regional agencies including the Aga Khan Agency for Habitat. Stated support comes from Geo Mountains and from the Glacier and Permafrost Hazards in Mountains standing group of the International Association of Cryospheric Sciences and the International Permafrost Association. Funding amounts and sources are not disclosed, no individuals are named, and the site is labelled beta. Cite it as a consortium finding attributed to the consortium; do not upgrade it to institutional authority.

open_threads.text: What standard of evidence the loss and damage fund applies to a claim from an event with no event-level attribution. The live question of the week and still unanswered, with a date on it for the first time. The board meets in its first-ever extraordinary session on 22 October on a draft decision that sets aside US$20 million provisionally and invites a proposal to be approved later — a construction that lets the board act without saying what standard it is applying. Meanwhile the ground moved underneath the claim: a reconstruction published on 13 October finds a forty-eight-day measurable precursor on the slope, which is the first serious counter to the adaptation-limits reasoning the claim would otherwise rest on. Eight weeks after Nepal's request, no board, bank, insurer or court has reasoned publicly from either finding.

Whether any part of the deltacommissaris's ask — 1 per cent of national output to at least 2 — survives into a government commitment. Fifth checkpoint passed in silence: no cabinet response to the 2027 programme against a one-day turnaround in 2025, and nothing on water in the responsible committee inside the week. The chamber was in session. The autumn budget rounds on infrastructure and water fall later, so some of this is still calendar; five checkpoints is well past the point where calendar explains it. The nearest external pressure remains the European framework of 28 October and its expected requirement of named risk owners.

Whether an adaptation-limits argument is adjudicable by the institutions that will receive it. Advanced, and not in the direction the thread anticipated. The argument now has a counter-argument from the research side rather than from an obligor: the mountain centre's reconstruction of 13 October finds the failure was preceded by forty-eight days of satellite-measurable deformation and recommends integrating satellite, seismic and hydrological monitoring with impact-based forecasting — the vocabulary of a soluble problem, against the attribution network's conclusion that the event exceeded the predictive limits of existing risk reduction. The first institution that has to choose between those two framings is the fund board on 22 October. The European framework of 28 October and its named risk owners remains the other route.

Who bears the privately held share of Nepal's losses, and whether a sovereign loss and damage claim can cover them. One figure advanced and it is still not a government document: Nepali officials are reported by a specialist wire as putting recovery and reconstruction at an estimated US$4.8 billion, which falls inside the US$4 to 5 billion range an earlier explainer gave and is the first version of the number attributed to officials rather than to commentary. The withdrawn NRs 559.18 billion figure is still not carried. The assessed split — about seventy per cent of about Rs408 billion on the private sector, with 759 MW of damaged generation — stands as the only sourced arithmetic, and the instrument on offer is US$20 million.

Whether any security institution reads the sea-level declaration as a security instrument. Nothing, in a week when two adjacent things happened. The Union adopted a negotiating mandate naming climate change a threat to peace and security without referring to the declaration; the Security Council's October programme still carries no climate, water, food-security or environment item in any framing, two-thirds through the month. The declaration was adopted by consensus seven weeks ago and no security institution has cited it.

Whether the alliance's removal of the climate referent from its resilience baseline is a drafting choice or standing practice. The test fell this week and returned a split answer. The alliance's own centre of excellence convened a summit titled around climate-smart investment, with nine tracks naming climate throughout, which is the centre saying climate freely while the binding requirements do not — the pattern the thread predicted, and evidence that the removal was a discipline applied to instruments that bind. But the centre has published nothing from the summit, so the free use of the word exists on a programme page rather than in any output. And the same operation has now been performed one level up by a different institution: the European Council's October conclusions discuss resilience, preparedness and the Arctic with no climate referent and no hazard referent either.
Whether money reaches Somalia before the October-to-December rains.
open_threads.resolution: Answered yes, in part, and the answer required correcting this digest. Money did move before the rains: $7 million was pre-approved from the central emergency response fund in June for flood response preparedness ahead of the El Niño, alongside $10 million for drought response, and on 24 September Britain announced £5 million specifically for Deyr flood preparedness, split equally between a health, nutrition, water and protection programme led by Action Against Hunger and a Shabelle-basin rehabilitation programme delivered through three agencies, expected to reach about 600,000 people. Last week's digest said the money had not come; it had, one day before that was written. The proportions still carry the original finding: about £5 million and $7 million of anticipatory money against 2.5 to 3.5 million people exposed, roughly a million expected to be displaced, and a humanitarian plan at about a quarter funded. What happens next — whether the forecast verifies and whether the anticipatory money measurably reduced loss — is carried forward as a new question rather than as this one.

open_threads.text: Whether India or China responds to Nepal's proposal for a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism, made from the General Assembly rostrum on 24 September. Fourth week, nothing from either capital — and this week the silence acquired a structural explanation rather than a diplomatic one. An Indian institute's report with a Dutch partner argues that South Asian climate cooperation is constrained by national and siloed governance, sovereignty and information-sharing sensitivities, and material asymmetries that make states facing one hazard set different priorities, so that proposals get designed for political feasibility rather than for the risk. On that account an unanswered regional proposal is the system's normal output. The one cooperative thing that did happen was technical and bilateral: a joint Himalayan field mission across the Nepal-China border.

Whether the joint United Nations climate-security programme's third phase has a stated funding requirement, and whether contributions are rising, flat or falling. Unchanged; the route remains identified and not taken. Nothing was found on the programme inside the week, in a week when the Union adopted a climate mandate naming peace and security and named no instrument to carry it. Ninth consecutive week in which the programme is either cited as evidence of commitment or not mentioned at all, by governments that have put US$18.27 million into it over nine years, with the Netherlands not among the fourteen contributors.

Whether the climate panel remains the reference science for climate decisions, on what timetable, and which states are pressing on each axis. Substantially reframed this week, and the reframing is a correction to this publication; the pushback sets it out. Nobody is proposing a substitute body in any forum. What is contested is the date: five consecutive plenaries have failed to decide whether the next assessment's working-group reports land before the 2028 stocktake or in 2029, four proposals remain on the table, and the panel's trust fund is reported heading for depletion before the cycle ends. The security stake is unchanged and is about dates rather than identity — the 2025 world-court opinion's best-available-science standard, the sea-level declaration's presumptions and the loss and damage fund's evidentiary practice would all run on a 2021-23 assessment for another cycle.

Whether any security institution treats the meteorological observing system's radio spectrum as an asset to be defended before the 2027 radiocommunication conference. Nothing new on spectrum, and an adjacent answer arrived from the opposite direction. The only pre-event evidence anyone has about the field's most-cited recent disaster came from a European civil earth-observation satellite, read seven weeks after the fact by an Asian research centre (B2). That is the clearest demonstration available of what a public observing system is for, and it was produced by nobody who thinks of themselves as defending one. The Union's adopted mandate of 12 October does make early-warning availability a key component of climate resilience, especially for small island developing states and least developed countries — the first time a Union negotiating position in this digest's run has said so — and says nothing about the observing system the warnings depend on.

Whether any public institution produces an estimate of what Europe's 2026 heat season cost, to set against the private one. Unchanged, and the deadline is now ten days away. The only figure in circulation remains an insurer's — about EUR 113 billion of annual output across thirty countries, from proprietary damage functions — and the statistical office, the environment agency and the national meteorological services have converted nothing. If the framework of 28 October stands up a climate insurance architecture without specifying an independent basis for loss estimation, the private number becomes the official one by default. Note what the attribution network did and did not publish this week: a study of a Pacific hurricane, and nothing on Europe's heat season since the ocean-temperature study of 19 August.

Whether the Somali Deyr forecast verifies and whether the anticipatory money measurably reduced loss. The first half is verifying. Mogadishu flooded on 12 October; the Shabelle at Jowhar has been above its high flood-risk level since 13 October at 5.36 m, fourteen centimetres below bankfull, with upstream rises of 2.21 m in four days and open river breakages spreading downstream; a ten-day forecast of 100 to 150 mm over the Jowhar catchment; flash floods already displacing households at Hudur. The second half has no instrument attached to it: no confirmation that the collective flood anticipatory-action framework or its trigger protocols are finalised, no district plans found, no figure for money moved against this event, and a Red Cross statement that preparedness and data are better than 2023 while funding and capacity have seriously decreased. The question is now the sharpest form of itself: the forecast was published in August, the river crossed its threshold on 13 October, and somebody knows how many of those days the money used.

Whether any candidate for Secretary-General states a position on climate, and in particular on Security Council competence over it. Sixth straw poll on 16 October, the first with colour-coded ballots separating permanent from elected members, seven candidates, none withdrawn, none new, no convergence: the leader on nine encourage with two permanent members against, two others on eight, one discouraged by all five. Nothing found on any candidate's climate position from the Council, the Assembly's dialogues or their own material. The week's one new input is a regional claim rather than a policy one — a Latin American and Caribbean letter of 13 October arguing it is the region's turn. Six polls, ten weeks to the end of the incumbent's term, and the question unasked in public.
Whether the climate panel's plenary at Addis Ababa, 12 to 16 October, decides the timetable for its next assessment, and on which side.
open_threads.resolution: Answered, and the answer is neither of the two sides. The plenary did not decide. On the evening of Friday 16 October the chair, Jim Skea, suspended the session after it had run past its scheduled close and after delegations from least developed countries and small island developing states had left, rather than put the question to the room; the panel's statement says the timelines for the three working-group contributions and the panel's budget both "remain open" and that deliberations will resume "at the earliest opportunity", with no date given. Both subsidiary questions are answered the same way: the review of the panel's own principles and procedures was deferred for a further session, and nothing was decided about the budget, which is the item with a hard deadline because the 2027 budget depends on it and the panel must reconvene before the end of the year to set one. This was the sixth consecutive session to fail on the timetable, and the last scheduled before the November conference opens the second global stocktake's information phase. Around thirty countries pressed for all three reports by about September 2028; China, India, Kenya, Russia and Saudi Arabia are reported on the side of delivery in 2029 for the impacts and mitigation reports. The thread closes because its question had a date and the date has passed. Its successor is ipcc-resumed-session-budget, because the live question is no longer which side wins but whether the body can convene to decide at all.

open_threads.text: Whether the Union's reported position that there is no scope for new climate finance commitments at the November conference survives into adopted conclusions, and whether it holds at Antalya.
open_threads.resolution: The first half is answered and the answer is yes in substance and no in wording, which is the more interesting outcome. Environment ministers adopted the conclusions on 12 October as document 14250/26. The reported phrase does not appear. What appears instead is an absence: no new figure, no new instrument, no new pledge, a cross-reference to the separate climate finance conclusions approved by finance ministers on 9 October, a restatement of the New Collective Quantified Goal and the global goal of at least US$300 billion a year by 2035, support for at least tripling adaptation finance by 2035, and the record that developed countries provided and mobilised US$132.8 billion in 2023 and US$136.7 billion in 2024. A position that commits nothing does not have to say so. The second question — whether the extension of the mitigation work programme to at least 2040 was what the line was traded for — is answered in the negative and this digest had it wrong: the word 2040 does not appear anywhere in the adopted text, which asks only for the programme to be continued and strengthened. What was actually traded away was international carbon credits, removed from the innovative-finance list amid member-state disagreement about their place in the emissions trading system; only carbon pricing survives. The thread closes here rather than at Antalya because the mandate is now fixed and the conference will test it rather than the question. One sentence from the same document outlives the thread and is carried into section B instead: paragraph 7 calls climate change an existential threat to humanity, ecosystems and biodiversity "as well as to peace and security".

open_threads.text: Whether the 1996 Ganges treaty is renewed, replaced or allowed to lapse, and on what terms. The date is now settled from the treaty text and the disagreement this digest reported between 12 and 31 December is resolved: the treaty was done at New Delhi on 12 December 1996 and Article XII gives it thirty years from signature, renewable by mutual consent, so it expires on 12 December 2026 and renewal is not automatic. The formula and the emergency clause are restated from the text in section C. The positions are unchanged and incompatible: India's external affairs ministry says all river matters run through the joint rivers commission and that technical meetings have continued; Bangladesh's water resources minister wants a new or revised treaty with an explicit guarantee of its share and expects completion before expiry; Dhaka has formed its own technical committee and reports approaching Delhi without response; West Bengal has a veto point. Eight weeks.
Whether anyone publishes how much anticipatory climate money has actually disbursed, as against pledged.
open_threads.resolution: Resolved against this digest. The figure exists and has been public since 28 May 2026, in the fourth annual global overview of anticipatory action produced by the Anticipation Hub with the UN food and agriculture agency, the UN humanitarian coordination office, the humanitarian start network, the food programme, the German Red Cross, the international federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent societies, their climate centre and a German development agency. For 2025: anticipatory action triggered 146 times across 54 countries, almost US$120 million released, 9.6 million people directly reached, 262 active frameworks against 154 the year before, a further 205 frameworks in development across 71 countries, and 57 countries described as institutionalising the approach; Germany and the European Union named as the largest contributors among donors who supplied data; money for acting before a hazard reported separately from money for building the systems. Three caveats travel with it and none of them restores the thread: "released" is the report's own verb and is self-reported by the implementing organisations, there is no independent audit or counterfactual, and there is no breakdown of how far ahead of impact the money actually moved. That last is the successor question and it is now carried as anticipatory-lead-time-figure. For the record of what the figure means: almost US$120 million worldwide in a year is about US$12.50 per person reached, and roughly nine thousandths of one per cent of the US$1.3 trillion a year by 2035 that the November conference will argue about.

open_threads.text: Whether solar radiation modification's arrival in government climate-security forums is a one-off or the start of an agenda. Unchanged on the government side and corrected on the institute side, where this digest had the format wrong. The American institute's private Arctic tabletop of 14 October has produced nothing public, but the same institute published in February 2026, from an earlier exercise in the same series, a named-author report modelling a 2030 Arctic stratospheric aerosol proposal — 3 teragrams of sulphur dioxide a year at 60 degrees north from 2035 to 2040, rising to a global peak of 14 by 2100 — built on a tabletop at New York Climate Week in September 2025 with more than twenty-five foreign and security policy experts, no team playing the United States, and no participants named. So the format does produce a record; what it withholds is the participant list. The report's own conclusions are the ones to watch for adoption: that states will default to geopolitical instincts rather than science, that Russia is the central risk, and that a trusted multilateral assessment is the precondition for anything. Still no state, alliance body or multilateral institution with a position on paper.

Whether the Pacific Islands Forum's own climate fund reaches its US$500 million initial capitalisation target by the end of 2026. Nothing new inside this week, and one arithmetic refinement from the pledging round that is worth recording because it does not match what this digest published. Tonga's prime minister said at the preparatory talks that "we still need US$320 million", which against the US$500 million target implies about US$180 million raised rather than the about US$190 million this digest carried. The longer-term goal is stated as US$1.5 billion. The declaration adopted at those talks commends the fund's establishment and calls on countries with the capacity to contribute; the next dated test is a conference session on small island states' finance needs at Antalya.

Whether US$1 million is the going rate for Dutch climate-security and climate-resilience money, or a floor the Netherlands happened to set at one venue. No new Dutch number this week, and the context against which to read it got sharper. The Netherlands agreed, in Council on 12 October, to a text calling climate change an existential threat to peace and security; its own ledger in the same week is a EUR 5 million annual defence line whose action plan is three months and fifteen days overdue, US$1 million to the Pacific fund, absence from the fourteen governments funding the UN's joint climate-security programme, a national briefing asked for by parliament and not yet held, and a national research interface that published nothing on the subject. The question is no longer about one pledge's size.

Whether the climate panel reconvenes before the end of 2026, what it decides about its 2027 budget, and whether the budget and the assessment timetable are taken together. The suspended session left both open and set no date. The budget is the item with a hard deadline, the panel's expenditures have been reported as exceeding contributions, and its largest-economy participant withdrew from participation and funding in January. If the two items are bundled when the session resumes, the group that can live without a 2028 assessment holds something the group that wants one needs, which is a worse configuration for the earlier timetable than this week's non-decision looks. Watch for a resumption date, for whether it falls before the November conference, and for any statement from either camp. A decision was wanted by the end of 2026.

Whether the forty-eight-day precursor signal on the slope above the Gyirong-Rasuwa corridor is treated as foreseeability by any institution that has to decide something. The measurement is up to 40 cm of satellite-measured line-of-sight movement between 7 July and 24 August 2026, published on 13 October by a research centre that also says it cannot predict when a collapse will happen. Four possible receivers: the loss and damage fund's board, which meets on 22 October on a claim from this event; an insurer or reinsurer pricing Himalayan hydropower, of which two projects have now been destroyed in seven weeks; a court, in a jurisdiction where a state or operator could be said to have had notice; and the national authorities who issued warnings twenty-five to thirty minutes after the debris passed. What makes it a general question rather than a local one is the symmetry: if measurability becomes the test, every unmonitored slope is a liability and every monitoring programme is a defence, which inverts the incentive the adaptation-limits argument creates.

Whether anyone publishes how far ahead of impact anticipatory money actually moves. The annual global count now gives the amount released — almost US$120 million across 146 activations in 54 countries in 2025 — and is self-reported by the implementing organisations, with no audit, no counterfactual and no lead-time breakdown. Lead time is the whole claim: forecast-based finance is distinguished from ordinary emergency relief by the days between the transfer and the impact, and nothing public counts them. The Somali Deyr is the natural experiment and it is now running — probabilities published in August, the river above its high flood-risk level on 13 October — so the numerator and denominator both exist somewhere. Alongside it, the evidence base on whether anticipatory transfers reduce loss remains a handful of quasi-experimental studies and working papers, which is thin for a doctrine this widely invoked.

Whether the first Dutch briefing on climate, nature and security is held during 2026, as a parliamentary motion asks, and whether that motion was in fact adopted. The amended motion, tabled on 3 March 2026 as 36800-XXIII-53 and replacing an earlier version of 12 February, asks the government to organise such a briefing with the national counter-terrorism and security coordinator and outside experts. Two things to establish, in order: the voting result, which the chamber's own listing does not show and which the published vote lists and stenographic record would settle; and whether anything is scheduled with ten weeks of the year left. This matters out of proportion to its size because it is the only dated Dutch ask on this subject this digest has found, and because the counter-terrorism coordinator would be the first Dutch security institution formally handed the file.

Whether the climate referent returns to a European Council conclusion in any substantive form. The October conclusions use the word three times in twenty-one pages — once on the carbon market, twice on member-state participation at a conference — while devoting a section to defence readiness and a paragraph to resilience, preparedness and critical infrastructure in which every named threat is a deliberate adversary act, and a paragraph to the Arctic as a security space with no driver named. Three dated tests follow. The integrated climate resilience framework on 28 October, which is a Commission instrument the heads of government did not mention. The special European Council on the long-term budget on 26 and 27 November. And the December European Council, which is where a December text can be counted the same way. The point of counting is that agenda separation is a weak observable and a ranking document is not an agenda.

open_moves.text: Denmark's Security Council food-security debate, outcome document unconfirmed. Unchanged and October is nearly closed: the month's programme carries no food-security item in any framing and the only remaining route is the joint seminar with the African Union on 21 and 22 October, where the framing would be the African Union's to bring. Worth noting against it that a famine risk was classified in Somalia this month and no Council member raised it.

The American climate-security institute's philanthropic-funding bet. Fourth consecutive week of movement in the same direction and the register has now changed completely. The week's one new item is an event announcement for 27 October, "Charging Forward: Electric Vehicles as Defense Technology", moderated by the institute's own director, arguing that advanced batteries are a chokepoint technology on a par with semiconductors, that China dominates the supply chain, and that without a domestic electric-vehicle market the United States risks ceding a technology central to its future military capability. No climate content in the framing; no climate research published; a fourth week without a state-level briefer; the parent's new fellowship on artificial intelligence and national security closing applications on 20 October. This is a serious argument in the register that is currently funded, and it is not this field.

The Abyei climate, peace and security report and the next peacekeeping mandate renewal. Unchanged. The Stockholm institute's climate-change-and-security publications list still ends at the August Abyei study with nothing for September or October, which under this digest's split rule is lead time from a research institute and not a finding. Four mandate renewals fall on 31 October and the Council's Africa items in late October remain where this resolves.
PIF security-declaration merger.

The European integrated framework for climate resilience. Still 28 October, now ten days out, and this week supplied the context that makes it the Union's real climate-security instrument by default. The negotiating mandate adopted on 12 October commits no new international finance; the heads of government on 15 and 16 October discussed resilience entirely in terms of hybrid attack and did not mention the framework at all. So the framework arrives as the only place where the Union's climate risk management is actually allocated: a 3C reference trajectory, named risk owners, member-state resilience plans conditioning access to Union funding, and an insurance architecture. Two things to read in it. Whether it specifies an independent basis for loss estimation, failing which an insurer's proprietary EUR 113 billion becomes the official European number. And whether named risk owners create an administrative respondent to an adaptation-limits claim, which is the only route this digest has identified for that question. The date has already moved once, from 20 to 28 October.

Succession to the Secretary-General. Advanced and still unresolved. A sixth straw poll on 16 October, the first with colour-coded ballots separating the five permanent members from the ten elected, with China and the United States as tellers: the leader on nine encourage and five discourage but opposed by two permanent members, two others on eight encourage and six discourage and also opposed by two, one discouraged by all five. Nobody withdrew, nobody new entered, and an analyst's reading is "a split decision with no P5 convergence". A regional claim entered on 13 October from the Latin American and Caribbean group. The incumbent's term ends on 31 December. For this field the finding is unchanged through six polls: no candidate has been asked a public question about climate or about Council competence over it. Recorded separately as this week's D5, because the colour-coding is itself a move.

The November conference of the parties at Antalya, 9 to 20 November, under a Turkiye-Australia presidency. Advanced on the European side and silent on the presidency's own. The Union's mandate is now adopted with no new finance in it and a paragraph calling climate change a threat to peace and security; the heads of government's only contribution was to insist that all member states be equally admitted to the venue, which reads as the resolution of a months-long question about invitations. From the host state itself: a record rainfall event in Istanbul from 13 October, described by its governor as the heaviest since records began in 1942, and no located statement from the environment, urbanisation and climate change ministry — which also holds the conference presidency — connecting it to anything. Three weeks out.

Whether overshoot is adopted as a planning premise by security institutions or stays inside the climate-policy system. Advanced quietly and in the Union's own adopted text: the conclusions of 12 October reiterate the aim of "bringing the temperature increase to or below 1.5C by the end of the century", which is overshoot language adopted as a negotiating position without being described as such, drawing on the UN environment programme's report of 2 October. No security institution has adopted the premise, which is the original question and still unanswered.

Whether the small island states' legal-character defence of 1.5C holds. Fourth consecutive week in which the position is carried by individual states rather than by the alliance: this week by the Marshall Islands' climate envoy at the suspended plenary, objecting to delay rather than defending a threshold, and by a regional caucus letter about geography. Treat the legal-character defence as not currently being prosecuted by anyone rather than as defeated.

Whether the pre-event-indications finding produces a funded glacier-hazard early-warning programme, and whether it can survive the China-Nepal data wall. Advanced sharply and from an unexpected quarter. The mountain centre's reconstruction of 13 October supplies the strongest pre-event indication yet found for any event in this digest's run — up to 40 cm of satellite-measured slope movement over forty-eight days — and recommends integrating satellite, seismic and hydrological monitoring with impact-based forecasting and cross-border information sharing. On the data wall, the one encouraging observable: a joint field mission with the centre's China office began this week on both sides of the border. Against that, the bilateral mechanism that would have to carry a state-level data question is two months past a commitment to meet, and Nepal's regional proposal is four weeks unanswered. Still no funding.

Whether Nepal's restriction of foreign search-and-rescue becomes a precedent or an episode. Superseded and closing next week unless something revives it. Nepal's posture is outward-facing in every direction: a sovereign claim about to receive the first disaster-specific decision in the loss and damage fund's history, a regional mechanism proposed from the Assembly rostrum, and a joint cross-border scientific mission under way.

Whether the climate convention secretariat's economic-security framing is picked up outside the climate-policy system, and in particular whether any European security institution adopts the formulation.
open_moves.resolution: Answered on both halves and not in the way the question expected. A European security institution did adopt a security framing: on 24 September the Union's High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy co-hosted a foreign ministers' dialogue on climate change and ecosystem degradation as national security risks. But it adopted this field's own formulation, national security risk, not the secretariat's economic-security substitution. And the secretary himself substituted again in the same week, telling Climate Week that electrification shields countries, families and businesses from fossil-fuel supply shocks and calling it a development strategy, an industrial strategy, a health strategy and a security strategy — security fourth, and meaning supply security. So the two moved past each other: the institution reached for the field's register in the same week the secretariat reached past it. The question is closed because its premise has been falsified. It assumed the secretariat's phrasing would be the vector by which the security frame travelled into European institutions, and the frame travelled without it.

open_moves.text: Whether the deltacommissaris's two-per-cent ask converts into any government commitment. Fifth checkpoint passed with silence: no cabinet response to the 2027 programme and nothing on water in the responsible committee, in a week when the chamber was sitting. The nearest pressure remains external and is now ten days off — the European framework of 28 October and its expected requirement of named risk owners, which is awkward for a governance model built on distributed responsibility.

Whether Nepal's reconstruction bill produces a loss and damage response, and on what evidentiary basis. Advanced for the first time in seven weeks and recorded as this week's D1. A draft decision reported on 16 October would have the board provisionally set aside US$20 million — one Kathmandu report gives US$21.6 million including US$1.6 million of oversight fees — and invite Nepal to submit a proposal for approval at a regular meeting, piloting a route for requests outside the fund's regular call. It is to be taken at the fund's first-ever extraordinary board meeting on 22 October, about forty-five days after the ministers wrote. The evidentiary basis is still not addressed: the draft is reported to mention neither attribution nor adaptation limits, and the ground underneath moved on 13 October. Context: 180 proposals worth about US$2.8 billion against about US$350 million available, nothing yet disbursed since 2022, and officials calling the figure symbolic against an estimated US$4.8 billion of recovery cost.
Whether the rescission was announced as expected, whether the endangerment-finding proposal followed, and whether the Houston ministerial's outcome document mentions climate.
open_moves.resolution: All three answered. The partial repeal of the carbon pollution standards for fossil-fuel-fired power plants was finalised on 14 September 2026 by Administrator Lee Zeldin, signed at the G20 Energy Abundance Ministerial in Houston rather than on its sidelines; the agency prices it at $310 billion in savings and calls it the largest power-sector deregulatory action in US history. The separate proposal followed simultaneously: EPA proposed rescinding every remaining greenhouse-gas standard for the sector, the vehicle for repealing the power-plant endangerment finding, with $370 million in claimed direct compliance-cost savings. And the ministerial's outcome document, a Critical Minerals Meeting Communiqué, does not mention climate: it grounds critical minerals in energy security, digital infrastructure, emerging technologies and economic development, and calls for voluntary and collaborative cooperation respecting national sovereignty and 'different domestic pathways'. Canada's own readout of the meeting likewise contains no reference to climate change. Environmental organisations have said they will litigate. The substitution this digest read off the ministerial's branding last week is confirmed in a negotiated multilateral text, which is why this closes as landed rather than as too early.

open_moves.text: Whether the alliance ever states what happened to the Secretary-General's annual climate and security assessment. Still no statement, and the displacing event has now been held: the centre of excellence's Montreal summit of 15 and 16 October, by invitation, on how to invest the climate-relevant share of a rising defence budget. The centre has published nothing about it as of 19 October, against recaps of the 2024 and 2025 editions within days of each. Recorded as this week's D4.

Whether the relocation of the evidentiary question from causation to adaptation limits is taken up by the institutions that have to apply it. The most consequential week yet and the news is not what the move expected. No fund board, bank, insurer or court has reasoned from adaptation limits, five weeks on. What happened instead is that the premise acquired a counter-argument from the research side: the mountain centre's reconstruction of 13 October finds a forty-eight-day measurable precursor on the slope, against the attribution network's conclusion that no early warning system could have given sufficient lead time. The network itself published this week on a Pacific hurricane and nothing on the Horn of Africa or on Europe's heat season. The first institution that must choose between the two framings is the fund board on 22 October.
Whether the American climate-security field's move to the state level is a durable relocation or a holding pattern.
open_moves.resolution: Answered no, and closed. Four consecutive weeks with no new state-level briefer since Ohio on 18 September; no state government named as commissioner or partner on any of the five; no second American institute writing for statehouses; and the institute's new programme capacity going elsewhere twice over — the parent's fellowship on artificial intelligence and national security, applications closing 20 October, and the institute's own event of 27 October on electric vehicles as defence technology. The statehouse series was one bet among several and it is not the one being pressed. The successor question is not where American climate-security work relocates geographically but which register it survives in, and on this month's evidence the answer is technology and supply-chain competition with China. That is carried by the csr-ccs-staffing move rather than as a new thread.

open_moves.text: Whether the asymmetry in the Dutch budget — flood defence funded, spatial adaptation and freshwater reduced over the longer term — survives the cabinet's response to the 2027 delta programme and the autumn estimates. No amendment and no cabinet response found; the parliamentary budget rounds on infrastructure and water fall later in the autumn, so this is still lead time. The defence side hardened again: the EUR 5 million structural climate-security line stands and the action plan that would spend it is three months and fifteen days overdue. One new instrument on the same lane, from March and not from this week: a motion asking the government to hold a first national briefing on climate, nature and security during 2026, whose adoption could not be confirmed.

The British, European and Kenyan foreign ministers' dialogue on climate change and ecosystem degradation as national security risks, 24 September. Four weeks on, no institutional follow-through from any of the three and nothing from the Union's external action service. What the Union did produce in the same period is a Council mandate naming climate change a threat to peace and security with no security institution mentioned anywhere in it — the formulation travelled into a text and not into any machinery. The service's climate envoy appears on the Montreal summit speaker list, in a role title no European source confirms.

Britain's GBP 331 million for climate-driven instability, of which GBP 330 million to the Global Environment Facility and GBP 1 million to the joint United Nations climate security unit. Nothing new this week from London. The standing finding holds and has become more interesting with the Dutch comparison: GBP 1 million was not the going rate for British climate money but the going rate for multilateral climate-security machinery specifically, ten times less than the GBP 10 million it put into an instrument the recipients control.

Nepal's proposal, from the General Assembly rostrum on 24 September, for a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism led by Nepal, India and China. Fourth week, no response from either capital, and this week the silence acquired an explanation that is not about either capital's disposition: an Indian institute's report with a Dutch partner argues that regional climate proposals in South Asia get designed for political feasibility rather than for the risk, and that sovereignty and information-sharing sensitivities shape what can be proposed at all. On that reading an unanswered proposal is the system working as it does. The one thing that did cross the border this week was a joint technical field mission.

The alliance's revision and first public release of its seven baseline requirements for resilience, 15 September. Nothing new from the alliance, and the test of whether the climate referent's removal was a drafting discipline returned a split answer: the centre of excellence's Montreal summit named climate throughout its own programme, which is the pattern predicted, but the centre published nothing from it, so the free use of the word exists on a programme page and nowhere else. The same operation has now been performed at Union level by the European Council, where neither the climate referent nor any hazard referent appears in the resilience and preparedness language.

Australia's Climate Week keynote on climate security as national security, 21 September, and the challenge to it from a former chief of defence asking where the plan is. Nothing new. Australia holds the presidency of negotiations at Antalya and the Union's adopted mandate is now the text its negotiators will meet; nothing Australian and security-framed was found inside the week. Keynote and chairmanship remain separate registers for the same minister.

Fiji's four-pillar position for the pre-conference talks, set out on 29 September. One arithmetic refinement from the pledging round: Tonga's prime minister said the region still needs US$320 million, which against the US$500 million target implies about US$180 million raised rather than the about US$190 million this digest carried. The science pillar remains untransacted and this week shows why in the sharpest possible form — the decision it was aimed at was taken, or rather not taken, in a scientific-governance plenary where the Pacific's position was carried by the Marshall Islands and the outcome was a suspension.

The American climate-security institute's private tabletop on the security dynamics of a fictional 2030 stratospheric aerosol deployment, 14 October. No acknowledgement, no output and no participants named, as expected — but the framing this digest attached to it was wrong and is corrected. The same institute published in February 2026, from an earlier exercise in the same series, a named-author report with a specified scenario and a named technical partner that built the simulator: 3 teragrams of sulphur dioxide a year over the Arctic at 60 degrees north from 2035 to 2040, rising to a global peak of 14 by 2100, against SSP2-4.5, from a tabletop at New York Climate Week in September 2025 with more than twenty-five foreign and security policy experts and no team playing the United States. So the format does produce a record; what it withholds is who was in the room. Its conclusions are the thing to watch for adoption: that states will default to geopolitical instinct rather than to science, that Russia is the central risk including disinformation framing the consortium as neo-colonial, that China may oppose publicly while benefiting privately, and that a trusted multilateral assessment is the precondition for any of it.

Greece's Security Council programme of work for October, announced 1 October. Two-thirds through the month and the finding holds: no climate, water, food-security or environment item in any framing. What the presidency has run instead is the succession, including the first colour-coded straw poll in the process's history on 16 October. The joint seminar with the African Union on 21 and 22 October is the only remaining route and the month closes on 31 October with four mandate renewals.

The Berlin climate and security conference of 6 October, hosted by the German foreign ministry with the institute that founded it. Open on the only question the format leaves — whether any defence ministry repeats the weaponisation claim — and nothing this week repeated it. One adjacent observable: the alliance's climate centre attended the 2025 Berlin conference and published a note about it on 23 October 2025; no equivalent note has appeared for 2026, which is consistent with a centre that currently publishes almost nothing rather than with a changed relationship.

The November conference presidency's pricing of the climate finance ask against the alliance's 5 per cent defence commitment, stated at Nadi on 8 October. Nobody took the comparison up in public this week, and the venue where the counter-argument is being built has now met: the alliance's own climate centre convened a two-day summit on 15 and 16 October titled around climate-smart investment on the road to 5 per cent, with tracks on climate-resilience metrics for defence procurement and on financing and costing climate-smart defence. That is the machinery for answering "spend on climate like you spend on defence" with "we already do, inside the 1.5 points". No output has been published from it. Resolves partly at Antalya.
The Union's draft negotiating position for the November conference, reported on 6 October from a copy seen by a financial wire, stating there is no scope for new climate finance commitments.
open_moves.resolution: Landed, in substance and not in wording. The conclusions were adopted by environment ministers in Luxembourg on 12 October as document 14250/26 under the Irish presidency, chaired by climate minister Darragh O'Brien. The reported phrase is not in the text; what is in the text is an absence of any new commitment, a cross-reference to the separate climate finance conclusions of 9 October, and a restatement of existing goals. The expected trade did not happen: the word 2040 appears nowhere, and the mitigation work programme is only to be continued and strengthened. What was traded away was international carbon credits, deleted from the innovative-finance list; only carbon pricing survives. Two things from the same document outlive this move and are carried forward instead. Its paragraph 7 calls climate change an existential threat to humanity, ecosystems and biodiversity "as well as to peace and security". And its paragraph 11 condemns Russia's war of aggression and reiterates concern about the Middle East, in the strategic framing of a climate mandate, with nothing joining either to anything climatic — which is the current limit of what the Union will assert, in a text revised five times.

open_moves.text: The loss and damage fund's board calling the first extraordinary meeting in its existence, for 22 October, on a draft decision to set aside US$20 million for Nepal provisionally and to pilot a route for funding requests outside its regular call. Open on three things: whether the out-of-cycle route is adopted with stated conditions or left ad hoc; whether any board paper says what standard of evidence a claim from an unattributed event must meet; and whether the figure is US$20 million or US$21.6 million including oversight fees.

The climate panel's chair suspending the sixty-fifth plenary rather than deciding the assessment timetable or the budget in a room the least developed countries and small island states had left. Open on whether the session resumes before the end of 2026, whether the budget and the timetable are bundled when it does, and whether a sixth consecutive non-decision is eventually recorded by anyone as the outcome the later-timetable group wanted.

An Indian institute's workshop report with a Dutch partner, published 12 October as Special Report 227, arguing that shared climate vulnerability in South Asia does not produce collective action because governance is national and siloed, sovereignty and information-sharing sensitivities constrain what can be proposed, and asymmetries make states facing one hazard set different priorities. Open on whether its nine observations are picked up by anyone designing a regional mechanism — Nepal's proposal being the live candidate — and on whether any Indian or Chinese official engages the argument.

The alliance climate centre's fifth Montreal climate security summit, 15 and 16 October, by invitation, titled around climate-smart investment on the road to 5 per cent, with nine tracks including climate-resilience metrics for defence procurement and the financing and costing of climate-smart defence, and a speaker list spanning allied armed forces, NATO divisions, European and American institutes, the external action service and the aerospace industry. Open on whether either host publishes anything at all from it, against same-period recaps of the 2024 and 2025 editions, and on whether procurement metrics emerge that would let resilience spending be booked against both the climate and the defence ledger.

The Security Council's first use of colour-coded ballots in a straw poll on the succession, on 16 October, separating the five permanent members from the ten elected so that a potential veto is visible without being attributable. Open on whether a seventh poll is held before the end of the year, whether colour-coding is retained, and — the only question that matters here — whether anyone asks any candidate a public question about climate or about Council competence over it before the choice is made.
